query: Why do resolution duration values vary across tickets?

per_column.name: incident_category
per_column.rationale: Categorizes tickets by type from short_description; provides a strong grouping axis for explaining duration variance. Sample readings (WiFi, VPN, database) are sound extractions.

per_column.name: failure_mode
per_column.rationale: Failure characterization is a useful axis for duration modeling. Most readings are warranted (connectivity, access_denied), but scope like 'full_outage'/'no_response'/'sync_failure' asserts operational detail not present in a terse short_description, so some values are weakly grounded inferences.

per_column.name: affected_system_type
per_column.rationale: System type is a reasonable grouping axis but heavily correlated with incident_category (VPN->vpn_server, database->database_server), so much of its leverage is redundant. Values are well grounded in the description text.

per_column.name: affected_scope
per_column.rationale: Scope (individual vs system_wide) is a genuinely useful driver of resolution time. However the source text rarely states scope; e.g. 'Cannot connect to office WiFi' labeled 'individual' and 'Printing issues in office' labeled 'location_specific' are confident inferences the terse text does not clearly support.

per_column.name: resolver_match
per_column.rationale: Presumably compares assigned_to vs closed_by/assigned_agent, potentially relevant to routing/duration. But grounding is questionable: row 1 shows resolver_match True with assigned_agent=Fred Luddy=closed_by, yet row 2 shows assigned_agent=Beth Anglin while closed_by=Charlie Whitherspoon and resolver_match=False — the derivation basis is inconsistent and partly unverifiable.

per_column.name: assigned_agent
per_column.rationale: Largely redundant with existing assigned_to/closed_by columns, adding little new axis. More seriously, produced values contradict the source: row 2 source closed_by=Charlie Whitherspoon but assigned_agent=Beth Anglin; row 5 closed_by=Luke Wilson but assigned_agent=Charlie Whitherspoon — apparent hallucinated/misattributed assignments.

per_column.name: open_hour_of_day
per_column.rationale: Time-of-day bucket derived correctly from opened_at (8:50->morning, 18:14->evening) gives a plausible new axis for duration variance (off-hours staffing).

per_column.name: caller_type
per_column.rationale: named_user vs itil_user could relate to priority/handling. But basis in source is unclear and possibly derived from caller_id not shown; row 2 'itil_user' vs others 'named_user' cannot be verified from provided text, so grounding is uncertain.

per_column.name: is_repeat_or_cluster_incident
per_column.rationale: Repeat/cluster status is analytically relevant, but with 461/500 flagged 'true' it is near-constant, reducing leverage. Grounding is weak: a single short_description does not reveal whether an incident is a repeat/cluster; these look like unsupported assertions.

judge.rationale: The added columns supply several genuine grouping axes for explaining resolution-duration variance: incident_category, failure_mode, affected_scope, and open_hour_of_day are the strongest and mostly well grounded in short_description/opened_at. affected_system_type is useful but largely redundant with incident_category. Grounding weaknesses cluster in inferred/relational columns: assigned_agent contradicts the source closed_by in two of five samples (apparent hallucination), resolver_match has an inconsistent derivation, affected_scope over-asserts scope from terse text, and is_repeat_or_cluster_incident is both near-constant and unsupported by single-row text. Overall the set clears the usefulness bar comfortably but has notable grounding lapses.
